1.outcome: Run rustc, Cargo and rustup successfully in a fresh terminal, and identify the job of each tool.
1.why: Before our world can contain a falling grain, the computer must be able to turn Rust source into a runnable program. Today we install that toolchain and prove it works. A successful download alone is not the finish line: a new terminal must find the commands and the native linker must be available.

sections.title: Begin with the terminal, not the installer
sections.html:
On your Mac, press Command–Space, type Terminal, and open it. The text before the cursor is the shell prompt; it is not part of a command. In a prompt such as (base) anujbarve@anujs-MacBook-Air rusty %, rusty is the current folder and % marks where you type. The (base) prefix usually comes from a Conda environment; it does not mean Rust is installed.

Type pwd and press Return. This prints the current working directory. Type rustc --version, cargo --version, and rustup --version, each on its own line. If all three report versions, skip installation and verify the active toolchain with rustup show active-toolchain. Do not overwrite a working setup simply to follow a video.

sections.title: What exactly are we installing?
sections.html:
The installer is rustup, which downloads and selects Rust toolchains. rustc is the Rust compiler: it translates source instructions into compiled output. cargo manages a package, builds dependencies, invokes the compiler, and runs development tasks. These tools work together, but they are not interchangeable.

Building a native executable also needs a linker and system development files. On macOS, check xcode-select -p. If the developer tools are missing, run xcode-select --install and complete the Apple dialog. This is separate from installing the full Xcode application. Keep this step visible in the recording: viewers often have Rust installed but cannot link their first executable.

sections.title: Install on macOS, then start a fresh shell
sections.html:
Use the official rustup command shown below. It downloads the installer over HTTPS and executes it in a shell. Read the installer prompts and choose the default stable installation unless you already have a deliberate toolchain setup. The installed files normally live under your user account, with command shims in $HOME/.cargo/bin.

After installation, close and reopen Terminal. Alternatively, for the current POSIX-style shell, run source "$HOME/.cargo/env". Then repeat all three version checks. The version strings and hashes will change over time; the important observation is that each command is found and reports its own version. command -v cargo tells you which executable the shell is resolving. If it points somewhere unexpected, inspect that before editing shell configuration blindly.

sections.title: Windows and Linux viewers: same tools, different native prerequisites
sections.html:
On Windows, use the installer linked from the official Rust installation page. Choose the documented MSVC setup and complete its Visual Studio C++ build tools requirements. Open a fresh PowerShell window and run the same version commands. Do not paste the macOS source command into PowerShell; its shell syntax is different.

On Linux, the rustup installation command is the same as macOS, but native development packages come from the distribution. Ubuntu commonly uses sudo apt update followed by sudo apt install build-essential; other distributions use their own package names and managers. Install only the prerequisites relevant to your system. The goal across platforms is identical: a compiler, Cargo, toolchain management, and a working native linker. The next lesson proves them together by compiling a real program.

sections.title: macOS command blocks: checks first, installation only if missing
sections.html:
Run this first block one line at a time. These are checks, not installation commands:

rustc --version
cargo --version
rustup --version
xcode-select -p

If the Rust commands already work, do not run the Rust installer. If Apple developer tools are missing, run the following and finish the Apple dialog:

xcode-select --install

Only when Rust is missing, use the official installer:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

Then reopen Terminal, or load the environment into this existing shell and verify again:

source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
rustc --version
cargo --version
rustup show active-toolchain

A version line proves the command is found; the next lesson compiles a program to prove the compiler and native linker work together.

exercises.prompt: Run command -v rustc and command -v cargo. What do the returned paths tell you?
exercises.hint: The shell searches PATH directories in order.
exercises.solution: Run the two commands and compare the results. A normal rustup setup resolves commands under your user’s .cargo/bin. The path explains which installed program receives your command; it does not describe the current game folder. If another installation appears first, record it and investigate before changing PATH.

exercises.hint: The installer normally updates shell startup configuration.
exercises.solution: A fresh shell should find the commands automatically. If it does not, activate the current shell with source "$HOME/.cargo/env", confirm that works, then inspect the startup file appropriate to your shell rather than repeatedly reinstalling Rust. The distinction is installed files versus shell command lookup.

exercises.title: Explain the chain for your episode
exercises.prompt: Without reading, explain what rustup, Cargo, rustc and the linker contribute.
exercises.hint: Installation, orchestration, compilation, and final executable assembly are separate jobs.
exercises.solution: A concise explanation is: rustup manages toolchains; Cargo coordinates package builds; rustc compiles Rust; the native linker combines compiled pieces and system libraries into a runnable executable. We installed the tools needed for that chain, but have not yet built our game.
exercises.proof: The explanation distinguishes all four roles instead of calling them all the compiler.

2.outcome: Create game/, edit its source, and compile and run your own first Rust executable.
2.why: We now have tools, but tools are not a game. This lesson connects one text file to a running executable. That edit–save–build–run cycle is the foundation of every episode, so we will inspect the folders and output rather than treating cargo run as a magic incantation.

sections.title: Create a package in the correct place
sections.html:
Start in Terminal at the rusty repository root. Check pwd and ls; you should recognize the course and docs folders. If you are elsewhere, use cd /Users/anujbarve/Documents/rusty on this Mac. Viewers must substitute their own checkout path. Then run cargo new game --vcs none. This creates a package called game without creating a nested Git repository.

If game/ already exists, stop and inspect it; do not delete or overwrite existing work. Enter the package with cd game. From now on, Cargo commands in these early lessons run here. The distinction matters: the repository root contains learning documents, while game/Cargo.toml identifies the executable package Cargo should build.

sections.title: Read the package before running it
sections.html:
Open Cargo.toml and src/main.rs in your editor. The manifest names the package, its version and Rust edition, followed by a dependencies section. Leave the edition generated by Cargo alone. The source file contains fn main(); for this small native executable, execution begins in that function. Its braces contain the body.

The generated println! call prints a line to the terminal. The exclamation mark identifies a macro invocation; you do not need to understand macro implementation yet. Change its string to the sandbox greeting below, then save the file. The terminal does not see unsaved editor buffers, so a visible edit in an editor is not yet proof that Cargo will compile it.

sections.title: Build, launch, and separate the kinds of output
sections.html:
Run cargo run. The first run normally prints Cargo messages such as Compiling, Finished and Running, followed by your program’s greeting. Cargo’s messages describe the build workflow; the greeting comes from your program. A later run with unchanged source may skip compilation. A changed source file causes the relevant build work to happen again.

The executable is placed under target/debug/ for the default development profile. On macOS/Linux, ./target/debug/game launches the already-built executable directly. Run it, then edit the greeting without rebuilding and launch that path again. It still prints the old greeting. This experiment makes the difference between source and compiled executable observable.

sections.title: Use the three everyday checks
sections.html:
Run cargo check, cargo fmt, and cargo run. Check asks whether the package passes compilation checking without producing the final runnable binary. Fmt rewrites formatting; it is not a correctness test. Run builds what is needed and launches the executable. We will add cargo test when we have behavior to verify.

Now remove one closing quote in the greeting and run check. Read the first diagnostic’s filename, line and message. Restore the quote and rerun. An error is feedback about a specific broken program, not a sign that your setup is ruined. In the video, leave this small failure visible: learning to navigate an error is more useful than presenting only flawless typing.

sections.title: The complete first-run terminal sequence
sections.html:
On your Mac, start at this repository path. Viewers should substitute their own checkout path. First check whether a game folder already exists; if so, inspect it rather than recreating it.

cd /Users/anujbarve/Documents/rusty
pwd
ls

For a new project, create and enter the package, then run the generated program:

cargo new game --vcs none
cd game
cargo run

The first program prints Hello, world!. Open src/main.rs, replace its contents with the worked source below and save it. Then run these commands from the same game/ folder:

cargo fmt
cargo check
cargo run

The final output now contains Our ecological sandbox begins here.. If it still prints the old greeting, confirm the edited file is saved and that the terminal is in the package containing that file. If Cargo says it cannot find Cargo.toml, check pwd and enter game/; do not reinstall Rust.

The braces delimit statements in the function.
The semicolon ends the println! statement.

exercises.prompt: Print the greeting and then Materials ready. on a second line.
exercises.hint: Each println! invocation emits its own line.

    println!("Our ecological sandbox begins here.");
    println!("Materials ready.");

Save src/main.rs and run cargo run from game/. The order of calls determines the order of lines.

exercises.prompt: Use cargo build, then launch the produced binary without cargo run.
exercises.hint: The default executable is inside target/debug.
exercises.solution:

On PowerShell the path is .\target\debug\game.exe. The direct launch does not rebuild source; that is why an edited greeting is not visible until a build occurs.

exercises.prompt: From the repository root, try cargo run and explain a missing-manifest error.
exercises.hint: Find the directory containing Cargo.toml.
exercises.solution: Return to the package using cd game, or from the repository root use cargo run --manifest-path game/Cargo.toml. Do not create a second package just to hide the directory mistake.
exercises.proof: The same package launches and no duplicate project is created.

troubleshooting.cause: The terminal is outside the package directory.
troubleshooting.fix: Use pwd, locate game/Cargo.toml, then cd game or pass --manifest-path.

3.outcome: Store a cell’s column and row in named values and calculate its drawing position.
3.why: A cell needs a remembered position before it can move. Hardcoding numbers everywhere would make a grain’s identity disappear into arithmetic. Bindings let us name the quantities first, then derive drawing coordinates from them.

sections.title: Begin with the quantity, not the keyword
sections.html:
Imagine a grain at column 12 and row 5. Those are two counts in our teaching grid. They are not screen pixels yet. A binding associates a name with a value: let column = 12;. Read it as “bind the value 12 to the name column.” The semicolon ends the statement. Naming both coordinates makes the program’s assumptions visible before we introduce graphics.

Rust can infer the integer type in this simple example. We will annotate types explicitly in the numeric-types lesson. Today the important relationship is that later expressions can use the binding’s name instead of repeating the original literal. If you change column in one place, every expression using that binding sees the value selected there.

sections.title: Follow the program in order
sections.html:
The two let statements execute before the print calls. println!("Cell: {column}, {row}"); inserts the named values into the formatted text. The punctuation inside the string is output; the braces name the values to insert. This formatting mechanism is not a variable declaration and does not change the stored values.

Trace the example aloud: first column receives 12, then row receives 5, then the first message uses both. We do not have a graphical cell yet; the terminal output is a small observable model of the state that a later renderer will read. Keep the trace short enough to do mentally before running the program.

sections.title: Derive pixels from cells
sections.html:
The design gives one simulation cell a width of four physical pixels. In our temporary low-DPI teaching window, drawing units match that footprint. The cell at column 0 starts at x=0; column 1 starts at x=4; column 2 starts at x=8. The pattern is multiplication: screen_x = column * cell_size.

For column 12, 12 times 4 gives 48. This is a derived position, not an independent fact to memorize. If we changed column to 13, the drawing position would become 52. If we changed cell_size instead, every grid step would be farther apart. Position and scale therefore deserve separate names. The production renderer will later make the physical/DPI distinction explicit.

sections.title: Make one controlled change at a time
sections.html:
Run the example, then change only column. Predict which printed values change. Restore it, change only row, and predict again. Finally introduce let cell_size = 4; and replace the repeated 4 in the expression. This is a small refactor: the output stays the same while the intent becomes clearer.

Do not add motion yet. A useful first lesson about variables ends with a stable mapping from named state to an observable result. Once you can change an input and correctly predict the output, the next lesson can ask why some bindings are allowed to change during execution and others are not.

Drawing position: 48, 20
explanation: cell_size is one shared conversion factor.
screen_x and screen_y are computed values, not special drawing commands.
println! lets us inspect state before a renderer exists.

exercises.hint: Change only the two input bindings.

exercises.prompt: Introduce cell_size if missing, set it temporarily to 8, then restore 4.
exercises.hint: The coordinate is a cell count; scale is another input.
exercises.solution: With column 12 and row 5, size 8 produces 96,40. Neither cell coordinate changes. Restore size 4 because the actual game style fixes the cell footprint; the temporary change was a units experiment.

exercises.prompt: Replace one use of column with colum and run cargo check.
exercises.hint: The compiler resolves exact names in scope.
exercises.solution: The misspelled name has no binding. Repair the use to column, rather than introducing a second accidental variable. Read the diagnostic’s location and possible suggestion.
exercises.proof: The repaired program compiles and the original output returns.

4.outcome: Use mutable state for a falling row and explain the compiler error when reassignment is forbidden.
4.why: Yesterday’s position was fixed for one run. Falling means the same piece of state must take a new value during that run. Rust makes that permission explicit with mut, which helps us distinguish fixed configuration from changing simulation state.

sections.title: Reassignment is different from choosing an initial value
sections.html:
In let row = 5;, the value 5 initializes the binding. A later row = 6; tries to assign a different value to that same binding. Rust rejects that reassignment unless the binding was declared mutable. Add mut between let and the name: let mut row = 5;.

The permission belongs to this binding. It does not make every value in the program mutable, and it does not automatically change row. It simply permits later assignments that satisfy the type rules. We still need an update statement telling the program what new value to store.

sections.title: Read the update as a state transition
sections.html:
row += 1; is shorthand for adding one to the current row and storing the result back. Starting from 5, the state after the statement is 6. A print before and after the assignment makes that transition visible. This is the smallest useful model of movement: read old position, calculate new position, store it.

Our temporary teaching grid counts rows downward, so increasing row means moving lower on screen. This sign is a convention, not a universal law of gravity. The final world design uses altitude increasing upward; later we will introduce an explicit conversion. For now, keep the prototype convention consistent instead of mixing altitude into the same variable.

sections.title: Use the compiler as an experiment
sections.html:
Run the working example, then remove mut and run cargo check. The error should identify reassignment to an immutable binding. Read the source location before applying a suggested repair. You intentionally created the invalid program, so the error confirms the rule you are testing.

Restore mut and keep the cell size immutable. We want positions to change as simulation proceeds, but the art design fixes cell size. Marking every binding mutable would compile in some cases, yet it would make that important distinction harder to see. Give each binding only the permission its job needs.

sections.title: Contrast reassignment with shadowing
sections.html:
Rust also permits another let statement with the same name, called shadowing. let row = row + 1; introduces a new binding, while row += 1; updates an existing mutable binding. They can produce the same printed number in a tiny example but express different intentions.

We will use mutation for persistent simulation state because the world evolves over many updates. Shadowing is useful for transformations such as parsing or converting an input into a more useful representation. Do not use shadowing merely to avoid understanding why an actual update needs mutable access. First describe whether you are replacing the state of a continuing object or naming a new transformed value.

exercises.title: Fall farther once
exercises.prompt: Move from row 5 to row 8 with one update statement.
exercises.hint: Change the amount added, not the initial value.
exercises.solution:

The result is row 8 and drawing y 32 when size is 4. This is one larger step, not three separate simulation updates.

exercises.title: Mutate one coordinate
exercises.prompt: Add an immutable column, then try to move it. Repair only the needed binding.
exercises.hint: Mutability is declared independently for each binding.
exercises.solution:

column += 1;

Keep cell_size immutable. The repair expresses that column, too, is changing state. There is no reason to give unrelated configuration mutation permission.
exercises.proof: Both coordinates can update while cell size remains immutable.

exercises.title: Compare shadowing
exercises.prompt: Rewrite a terminal-only version using let row = row + 1 and explain the difference.
exercises.hint: Another let introduces another binding.
exercises.solution: Shadowing creates a new binding initialized from the old value. Mutation changes the value associated with the existing mutable binding. For persistent cell state, return to the mutable version before the next lesson.
exercises.proof: Your explanation describes binding identity, not only the final printed number.

troubleshooting.fix: Add mut to the binding whose state must change, then rerun check.

troubleshooting.fix: Keep executable statements inside main’s braces.

5.outcome: Distinguish integer grid coordinates, floating-point drawing units and elapsed seconds without accidental type or unit mixing.
5.why: A number alone does not explain what it measures. Column 12 is a cell count; drawing x 48.0 is a position in drawing units; 0.05 is a duration in seconds. Types and names help us keep those meanings separate before movement bugs become visually confusing.

sections.title: Whole positions belong to an integer grid
sections.html:
A grid coordinate identifies a particular cell. Between column 12 and column 13 there is no half-cell storage slot in this model, so we begin with i32, a signed 32-bit integer. Signed values will later let the world extend to negative columns. The annotation appears after the name: let column: i32 = 12;.

Integer storage has a finite range. We are not proving an unlimited-coordinate world by choosing i32; production coordinate range is an architectural decision. Here the type is large enough for our teaching fixture and makes the valid meaning clear. Small examples should expose boundaries rather than silently claiming infinite precision.

sections.title: Drawing asks for a different representation
sections.html:
macroquad drawing functions take floating-point values for coordinates and sizes. A float can represent fractional values, which suits drawing transformations and measured durations. f32 is a 32-bit floating-point type. The literal 4.0 makes our drawing size a fractional-capable quantity rather than an integer count.

Rust does not silently convert every integer argument into a float when an API expects one. At the drawing boundary, convert deliberately: column as f32 * cell_size. The grid remains integer based; only its presentation becomes a drawing coordinate. This helps preserve exact occupancy while letting the rendering API use its required representation.

sections.title: Type correctness is necessary, not sufficient
sections.html:
Both row and column may be i32, yet swapping them is still a semantic error. Likewise two f32 values can measure seconds and pixels, and multiplying or adding them carelessly can compile while making no sense. Names such as elapsed_seconds and screen_x carry information the primitive type alone cannot encode.

For this lesson, inspect each expression by asking “what does its input count, and what does its output measure?” Cell count multiplied by pixels per cell gives a pixel position. Adding elapsed seconds directly to a row would mix meanings. Later, narrower structs and interfaces can strengthen these boundaries; clear naming is the first inexpensive step.

sections.title: Use conversions deliberately and test their limits
sections.html:
The small teaching coordinates convert exactly to f32, but casts are not a general promise that all integers retain their precision as floats. Large integers can lose detail in floating-point representation. Keep world coordinates in their integer form for simulation and subtract camera origin before drawing when the world becomes large.

Try assigning 12.5 to an i32 binding and read the error. Then try 12 in an explicitly f32 binding and repair it to 12.0. These controlled failures distinguish type compatibility from a runtime calculation. Do not silence them with arbitrary casts until you can explain why the conversion is appropriate at that boundary.

Tick duration: 0.05 seconds. Default float formatting need not print a trailing .0.
explanation: The conversion happens where discrete state becomes presentation.

Printed formatting is not the stored numeric type.

exercises.title: Find the boundary
exercises.prompt: Label every number in the example as cells, pixels per cell, drawing units or seconds.
exercises.hint: The same primitive type can represent different units.
exercises.solution: column and row count cells. cell_size measures drawing units per cell in the low-DPI prototype. screen_x and screen_y measure drawing position. tick_seconds measures elapsed time. Only the coordinate-to-drawing calculation should combine the coordinate count and scale.
exercises.proof: No number is described merely as a float without its meaning.

exercises.title: Repair a type mismatch
exercises.prompt: Assign 12.5 to column: i32, run check, and fix the model without rounding the grid silently.
exercises.hint: A cell index is a discrete position.
exercises.solution: Use an integer column for occupancy. If you need a fractional visual offset, store a separate drawing value. Changing the simulation coordinate to a float would alter the model; it is not a harmless compiler-error repair.
exercises.proof: The grid coordinate remains integer and the program compiles.

exercises.title: Compute another position
exercises.prompt: Use column -2 and row 9 with cell size 4.0. Predict both results.
exercises.hint: Signed coordinates can be negative even before our view supports them.
exercises.solution: The conversion yields -8 and 36. A negative drawing x may lie outside the window; that is a visibility question, not an invalid arithmetic operation.
exercises.proof: Your prediction separates numeric validity from on-screen visibility.

troubleshooting.cause: The literal or API argument has the wrong numeric representation.

6.outcome: Write and call a small typed function that converts a cell coordinate into a drawing coordinate.
6.why: Once we calculate drawing positions in several places, repeated arithmetic becomes a maintenance risk. A function gives one calculation a name and a contract: what input it accepts and what output it returns. We can discover the function by first noticing the duplication it removes.

sections.title: Find the repeated operation
sections.html:
Both drawing x and drawing y multiply a cell coordinate by four. If those formulas drift apart, the grid stretches differently in each direction. Rather than maintaining two copies, name the operation screen_position. The function is useful because its job is small enough to explain in one sentence: convert one cell coordinate to a drawing coordinate at the current teaching scale.

This is not a reason to create a large utility module yet. First extract the exact repeated computation and keep its inputs explicit. A good first function lets us reason about behavior independently of whatever code happens to call it.

sections.title: Read the signature as an interface
sections.html:
fn screen_position(cell: i32) -> f32 declares a function, names one parameter and gives the return type. The parameter binding exists inside the function body. Calling screen_position(12) supplies an argument; inside that call, cell has the value 12. The caller’s variable name need not match the parameter name.

The signature says something testable before we read the body. It accepts an integer coordinate and produces a float. It does not draw a rectangle, change the caller’s coordinate, or open a window. Those would be additional effects and would deserve a different explanation.

sections.title: Expressions can be returned directly
sections.html:
In Rust, a function body can end with an expression whose value becomes the return value. Here the final expression is cell as f32 * 4.0 with no semicolon. Adding a semicolon turns it into a statement that discards that expression’s value; the function would no longer return the required f32.

You may also write return cell as f32 * 4.0;, but the final-expression style is common and concise. Do not memorize a rule that semicolons are always bad: statements such as println! calls and assignments still use them. Ask whether this expression is meant to supply a value to the surrounding function.

sections.title: Call it from more than one context
sections.html:
Use the function for column and row, then call it with a literal directly. Print the results in a terminal before returning to graphics. This isolates the conversion from window setup and makes testing cheap. Change a coordinate and predict the output; there is no hidden state in this helper.

The fixed 4.0 is acceptable for this tiny teaching slice, but it is a design assumption. When the renderer gains an art buffer and DPI conversion, the boundary may need a richer transform or an explicit scale parameter. A function makes that later change localized; it does not make the current assumption universal forever.

7.outcome: Use a boolean condition to distinguish a falling grain from a grain already resting above a floor.
7.why: Movement is not merely adding to a coordinate. A grain must first decide whether the proposed region is available. An if condition gives us the first explicit rule in the simulation: above the landing row it may move; at the landing row it must rest.

sections.title: Define the boundary in cell units
sections.html:
Let floor_row be 160, meaning the floor starts at grid row 160. A grain occupies one row of cells. Its highest allowed top row is therefore 159: occupying row 160 would overlap the floor. This one-row offset follows from the footprint, not from a mysterious correction constant.

Keep floor_row in cell units, not drawing pixels. The renderer later multiplies it by four. If you compare row 159 to a floor drawing coordinate of 640, the code may compile because both are integers, yet the comparison would use incompatible meanings. State the units before writing the condition.

sections.title: A comparison produces a boolean
sections.html:
The expression row < floor_row - 1 asks whether the grain is above its last legal row. It evaluates to a bool: true or false. if uses that result to choose which branch executes. When row is 158, the comparison is true; at 159 it is false.

The comparison does not itself change row. It is a question about the present state. This distinction will become important when we add a proposed movement distance: “currently above the floor” is different from “the entire proposed path is clear.” Today we isolate the first question with printed output.

sections.title: Trace both branches, including equality
sections.html:
Run the example with row 158, then 159, then 160. The first should report moving; the latter two use the non-moving branch. But row 160 is already invalid input for this fixture, not a legitimate resting position. A branch choosing not to move cannot repair every invalid starting state automatically.

Try changing < to <= and examine the equality case. The modified condition treats row 159 as movable, which can allow overlap if you later add a step. Boundary tests are useful because the difference between two comparison operators is often invisible in the middle of the world.

sections.title: Use a terminal decision before graphical motion
sections.html:
A printed word is enough to verify the condition today. We will later turn the branch into a mutation and add destination clamping or path inspection. Separating decision from movement keeps the source of an error visible: first establish what counts as blocked, then implement what happens when free.

For the episode, draw three simple cell rows or use the verified diagram: a grain above the landing row, a grain touching the floor, and an invalid grain overlapping it. Ask viewers to predict the condition result before running. This is a small piece of simulation reasoning they can reuse for walls, liquids and brush bounds.

8.outcome: Trace a finite loop and identify exactly what makes it terminate.
8.why: A frame loop will repeat while the game window exists. Before that, we need a repeatable experiment small enough to trace completely. A finite while loop lets us see how a condition and a state update cooperate to produce several steps rather than one.

sections.title: Replace repeated typing with a rule
sections.html:
We could write row += 1 three times, but the structure would hide the condition that decides how many steps are needed. A while loop expresses “repeat while this condition is true.” Starting at row 5 and continuing while row < 8 produces updates to 6,7,8. The body runs only after the condition is checked.

This order matters. If row already starts at 8, the body runs zero times. A loop is not a promise to perform at least one update; that depends on the construct and condition. Trace the initial check as well as the body when predicting output.

sections.title: Keep a state table beside the code
sections.html:
Before running, make three columns: row before the condition, condition result, and row after the body. The first row is 5,true,6; next 6,true,7; next 7,true,8; finally 8,false,no body. The printed lines appear after the increment, so they are 6,7,8 rather than 5,6,7.

This table is an execution trace. It is a way to discover where a mistaken prediction came from instead of randomly changing code. The same method later explains why an in-place grid scan can update one grain twice: track the state before each iteration, not merely the list of source statements.

sections.title: Remove the progress and observe the consequence
sections.html:
Temporarily remove row += 1. The condition remains true forever because row never changes. The terminal prints repeatedly and cargo run does not return. Stop the process with Ctrl+C. This experiment is intentionally small; do not leave an uncontrolled printing loop running while changing unrelated settings.

Restore the increment and verify termination. A loop generally needs some reason its condition will eventually become false, or a deliberate external exit policy. A game’s main loop is intentionally ongoing, but it must yield to the window framework so input and closing events can be processed. That is the next lesson’s different kind of repetition.

sections.title: Separate an update loop from elapsed time
sections.html:
The finite loop below runs as quickly as the CPU executes it. It does not mean one step per second, one tick per frame, or a physically meaningful falling rate. Repetition and timing are separate problems. We will later add an accumulator that decides when an update is due.

For now, the win is being able to predict iteration count and state changes. Try a different starting row and a step of two. Ask what happens when the step jumps past the limit. These variations prepare you to reason about clamping and overshoot without needing a graphical debugger.

9.outcome: Launch a responsive 1280×720 window with the game’s dark-sky base colour.
9.why: Our program can already hold and update state, but it only speaks through terminal lines. macroquad provides a window and drawing API so the same Rust code can begin showing the world. We will inspect the minimal frame loop instead of pasting an unexplained game engine.

sections.title: Add the dependency in the manifest
sections.html:
Open game/Cargo.toml. Under its existing [dependencies] heading, add macroquad = "=0.4.16". The leading equals sign pins this direct dependency to the version used by the design. Do not add a second dependencies heading. Save the manifest and source before running Cargo.

The first build downloads and compiles dependencies, so it can take longer than our terminal-only examples. Cargo.lock records resolved dependency versions and should be kept with this application. A downloaded crate is library code available to the package; it does not replace Rust’s compiler or create a window until our program calls into it.

sections.title: Read the configuration as data
sections.html:
The window_conf function returns a Conf value with named settings. Width and height choose the teaching window’s size. high_dpi:false and window_resizable:false deliberately simplify the first pixel mapping. sample_count:1 avoids multisample edge smoothing in this example. The remaining fields come from Default::default().

The title uses .to_owned() to provide the owned string expected by the configuration. Treat that as a named conversion at the API boundary for now; ownership will be explored directly in the next few modules. These restrictions are scaffolding, not changes to the final game’s resizable, DPI-aware design.

sections.title: Follow one complete frame
sections.html:
The attribute above main connects our entry point to macroquad and supplies the configuration function. Inside main, loop repeats the frame body. First clear_background fills the new frame. Then next_frame().await yields control to the framework so the frame can be presented and events processed.

Without that yield, a tight endless loop would prevent normal progression. The async spelling belongs to macroquad’s entry API; full asynchronous Rust is not a prerequisite for drawing the first frame. Learn the narrow contract: this awaited call hands control back between frames. We will keep simulation timing separate later rather than assuming one loop iteration equals a fixed amount of game time.

sections.title: Run and observe the boundary between code and operating system
sections.html:
Replace src/main.rs with the worked example, run cargo check, then cargo run. A dark window should open. Move it, close it through the operating system, and verify the terminal returns. Change only the title, rebuild, and confirm the visible change.

The colour channels 15,26,51 encode the reference night colour #0f1a33; alpha 255 makes it fully opaque. This is a flat teaching background, not the final sky ramp. If the native window fails, preserve the actual error and OS details. A successful compilation does not prove that every GPU, driver or display mode can create the graphics context; the M0 hardware gate exists for that reason.

10.outcome: Draw a crisp four-by-four pixel sand cell at a position derived from grid coordinates.
10.why: An empty window proves the graphics setup, but the first visible piece of our game is a cell. We will connect the named state from earlier lessons to rectangle arguments, keeping position, size and colour separate so none becomes an unexplained magic value.

sections.title: Place drawing between clear and present
sections.html:
In the window loop, draw_rectangle must run after clear_background and before next_frame().await. Clearing after drawing would erase the cell; drawing after the yield belongs to the next loop’s timing and makes the structure harder to understand. State the order aloud: background, objects, yield.

The rectangle API accepts x, y, width, height and colour. x and y identify the top-left drawing position under this simple default camera. Width and height determine the footprint independently. A rectangle at x=48 with width=4 occupies a small region beginning there; x is not the right edge and width is not a second coordinate.

sections.title: Derive the location from a cell coordinate
sections.html:
Use column 12 and row 5. Multiply both by 4.0 after converting the integer coordinates to f32. The resulting drawing origin is 48,20. This conversion reuses the units reasoning we established in the terminal, so graphics does not introduce a different coordinate system by surprise.

The design distinguishes physical screen pixels, art pixels and simulation cells. Here one simulation cell occupies four by four physical pixels in our low-DPI teaching window. Later it will contain two by two art pixels, which are presented at twice their size. Today the rectangle is an occupancy footprint, not a claim that one cell is one display pixel.

sections.title: Use one flat material colour
sections.html:
The sand base colour is RGB 226,182,121. Draw it with full opacity and no outline, gradient, noise or glow. A flat block makes its exact footprint easy to inspect and respects the visual direction. Do not add shadows or texture simply because the example looks small. The point is to establish the unit that thousands of cells will share.

Move column to 13 and predict the horizontal displacement: four drawing units. Change row instead and predict vertical movement. When this fails, inspect conversion arguments before blaming the renderer. Separating x/y position from size makes those failures easy to locate.

sections.title: Keep state stable across redraws
sections.html:
For this still example, column and row can remain immutable outside the loop. Each frame reads the same values and redraws the same cell. Drawing does not store a persistent grain in the canvas; the program owns state and reconstructs its presentation.

If you place the state declarations inside the loop, this static result still looks correct, which can conceal a later bug. Once movement is added, reconstructing initial state each frame will reset it. Introduce the right lifetime now by declaring the coordinates before the loop, then drawing from them inside. We will group those coordinates into a Cell struct next.

11.outcome: Define a Cell struct and keep its named coordinate fields together across frames.
11.why: A single grain can survive as two loose variables. Multiple grains, reset functions and simulation updates will make that fragile. A struct lets us express “these coordinates belong to one cell” as a type rather than relying on matching variable names by convention.

sections.title: Find the relationship we want to preserve
sections.html:
column and row are not two unrelated settings; together they describe one position. A struct groups fields into one value. Define struct Cell { column: i32, row: i32 } above main. This declaration describes a type; it does not create a grain or allocate a whole world.

Construct an instance with Cell { column: 12, row: 5 }. Field names make the inputs visible and reduce the chance of accidentally reversing coordinate arguments. The variable that receives this value now represents the complete teaching cell. Adding a material later will extend the same explicit state model.

sections.title: Type definition and value construction are different steps
sections.html:
The struct declaration lists each field’s type. A construction supplies an actual value for each field. Field order can differ during named construction, but every required field must be supplied unless a deliberate update/default pattern is used. We are not introducing that shortcut here; writing both fields keeps the first instance clear.

Access a field with dot syntax, such as cell.row. A field is not a function call: there are no parentheses. Start in the terminal by printing both fields, then replace the loose drawing variables with these accesses. This keeps the new syntax separate from the already-working window API.

sections.title: Decide where the value should live
sections.html:
The state belongs outside the frame loop because its lifetime spans many redraws. Declare let mut cell when you plan to update its fields, then draw from cell.column and cell.row inside the loop. Mutable ownership permits field changes such as cell.row += 1.

Do not derive Copy just because the struct is small. Our next lesson deliberately passes a custom struct by value and observes its move behavior. That will give borrowing a concrete purpose. For now, the owner in main stores one value, and dot access makes the relation between the coordinates visible.

sections.title: Keep the model small enough to explain
sections.html:
This Cell has only coordinates; it is a teaching representation of one visible grain, not the final eight-byte simulation cell. The production design stores coordinates implicitly in grid/chunk location and stores material state in each slot. We will change the representation when a grid exists.

That change is normal. We introduce a struct because it solves the present problem of coherent state, not because every later engine must store a position in every cell. End the episode by changing only row and confirming column remains unchanged. The viewer should see a named, inspectable value rather than an unexplained architecture diagram.

12.outcome: Recognize a moved-value diagnostic and distinguish a non-Copy struct from copied numeric values.
12.why: We want to pass a cell into a drawing helper, then use it again next frame. Passing the whole value by ownership would prevent that for our custom non-Copy type. Rather than introducing borrowing as arbitrary punctuation, we first build the precise problem it solves.

sections.title: Ask who owns the value after the call
sections.html:
The function consume_cell(cell: Cell) accepts a Cell by value. Calling it transfers ownership of our custom Cell into the parameter. The caller cannot then use its original binding as though that owned value remained available. This is why the final print in the example is rejected.

The compiler diagnoses the issue before running the program. Nothing partially executes and then fails at the print; compilation fails. That distinction matters when reading terminal output: a compiler error is not a runtime exception from a half-completed simulation.

sections.title: Make the failure small and intentional
sections.html:
Run cargo check on the worked example and look for the use-of-moved-value diagnostic, commonly E0382. Read the highlighted first move and later attempted use. The diagnostic links two source locations because the rule concerns a relationship across time, not merely one invalid token.

Do not immediately add Clone or Copy. First explain what each call is intended to do. A consumer that deliberately takes ownership may be correct. A drawing function that only needs to inspect should not consume the persistent state. That design intent is what will guide the borrowing repair in the next lesson.

sections.title: Why did integers appear to work differently?
sections.html:
An i32 implements Copy, so passing it by value copies the value and leaves the caller’s value usable. Our Cell has not implemented Copy; being small does not automatically grant that trait. Replacing the struct with an integer changes the type capability, not the ownership rule’s consistency.

A move is a semantic transfer of ownership; do not equate it with a guaranteed physical memory relocation. Compiler optimizations may eliminate or rearrange machine operations. At the source level, the important promise is which binding may be used after the transfer. That is the model the borrow checker verifies.

sections.title: Choose the interface from the job
sections.html:
Drawing needs temporary read access while main keeps ownership. Reset needs temporary write access to that same original. Neither task requires consuming the Cell. A future channel message or particle list, by contrast, may deliberately transfer ownership to another subsystem. Ownership is useful control, not simply an obstacle to bypass.

For this episode, show the failing program first, narrate the two relevant source locations, and compare a small i32 function. Stop at explaining why the API is wrong for drawing. The next lesson introduces references as the motivated repair; keeping the lessons separate prevents several unexplained changes from landing at once.

13.outcome: Use shared and mutable references so helpers inspect or update a cell without taking ownership.
13.why: The drawing helper should be allowed to read the cell, while reset should change it. In both cases main must keep ownership for the next frame. References express those access contracts directly, solving the moved-value problem we just observed.

sections.title: Borrow instead of transfer
sections.html:
Change a read-only function parameter from Cell to &Cell. At the call, write &cell to create a shared reference. The helper receives access to an owned value elsewhere; it does not become the owner of the Cell. After the call, main can still use the cell.

References are not copied world snapshots. They refer to the same underlying value for their valid lifetime. Dot access can read fields through a reference conveniently. This is why a rendering helper can inspect a large world without cloning the world every frame. The interface says it only needs a view.

sections.title: Mutation needs a different permission
sections.html:
A reset helper changes the original row, so its parameter is &mut Cell and the call supplies &mut cell. The owner binding must also be mutable. These two uses of mut are related but occur at different places: one permits the owner’s state to change, the other requests exclusive mutable access during the borrow.

A shared reference does not permit ordinary field mutation. Try assigning row inside inspect_cell and observe the rejection, then undo it. Do not make every helper mutable just to avoid deciding what it does. Narrow permissions help readers and the compiler reason about whether a call can change simulation state.

sections.title: Reason about when access overlaps
sections.html:
Rust permits multiple shared borrows while they are used, or an exclusive mutable borrow while it is used; conflicting access cannot overlap. This protects the same value from incompatible operations. A simple sequence of inspect, reset, inspect works because the calls do not need conflicting simultaneous access.

Do not teach that every borrow lasts until the closing brace of main. The compiler can end a borrow after its last use. To observe the distinction, store a shared reference, read it, then mutate after its final use. Next add another read of that old reference after the mutation and inspect the conflict diagnostic.

sections.title: Connect the contracts back to the window
sections.html:
The terminal experiment below isolates borrowing syntax. Once it is understood, make draw_cell accept &Cell, keep let mut cell before the frame loop, and call reset_cell(&mut cell) when R is pressed. Draw with draw_cell(&cell) each frame. State remains in one owner; helpers receive only the access they need.

This is the core pattern we will reuse for world rendering and simulation updates. The concept is not “Rust makes me type ampersands.” The reason is that different operations need different temporary access to one persistent object. End by asking which helper can change the row before reading its body; the signatures should already answer that question.

14.outcome: Schedule a simple 1x simulation update every 0.05 seconds independently of drawing frequency.
14.why: If we add one row every rendered frame, a 120 FPS display runs movement four times as fast as a 30 FPS display. A simulation tick must therefore be scheduled from elapsed time, not counted redraws. We can derive the accumulator from the need to remember incomplete time between frames.

sections.title: Separate showing the state from changing it
sections.html:
The renderer may draw the same row several times between simulation updates. That is correct: drawing answers “what does the world look like now?” while a tick answers “what is the next world state?” At a baseline 20 ticks per second, the desired period is 1/20 second, or 0.05 seconds.

The target is not one tick every three frames. That ratio happens only when rendering is exactly 60 FPS. At a different display rate, the number of redraws per update changes while the intended real-time tick rate stays the same. Treat any frame-count shortcut as a deliberate broken experiment rather than production timing.

sections.title: Remember the unspent fraction
sections.html:
get_frame_time supplies elapsed seconds since the preceding frame in macroquad. Add it to an elapsed accumulator. Whenever elapsed is at least 0.05, perform a tick and subtract 0.05. Do not set elapsed to zero after every tick: that discards the leftover fraction and slows the simulation under ordinary frame variation.

For two frames of 0.03 seconds, the first leaves 0.03 and runs no tick. The second brings the total to 0.06; one tick spends 0.05 and leaves 0.01. This trace is the reason for an accumulator. No special clock vocabulary is needed until the unspent-time problem is clear.

sections.title: Handle more than one due update
sections.html:
Use while rather than if when enough time may have accumulated for multiple updates. This teaching example caps catch-up at two ticks per rendered frame, then discards excess whole periods while retaining the fractional remainder. The policy deliberately slows the demo after a large stall instead of producing an unbounded catch-up burst.

This is not the final production scheduler. It has no calendar counter, fast-forward multiplier, pause policy or measured per-frame time budget. The production chapter will introduce those choices explicitly. For now, a bounded accumulator is enough to learn why physics updates and display frames are different units of work.

sections.title: Verify with synthetic time before a live window
sections.html:
A timing bug is easier to test when elapsed durations are inputs instead of actual sleeps. Then copy the same structure into the graphical loop using get_frame_time.

Keep the Cell outside the rendering loop and call the mutation helper only inside the due-tick body. Rendering remains outside that body so even frames with zero updates still display the latest state. A synchronous tick still consumes real CPU time; reducing TPS does not give permission for one tick to freeze rendering for 50 milliseconds.

15.outcome: Land one falling cell exactly above a floor without crossing it, even on a larger final step.
15.why: We have a timed update and a visible cell, but movement must respect geometry. A flat floor is the smallest collision fixture that reveals why checking the starting position is not enough: a three-row step can begin legally and end inside the obstacle.

sections.title: Derive the legal destination
sections.html:
If the floor begins at row 160 and the grain occupies one cell row, its top row may reach 159. Suppose it begins at 158 and proposes moving three rows: the unconstrained destination is 161, which overlaps the floor. The legal result is the smaller of the proposed destination and the last free row.

That gives (cell.row + 3).min(floor_row - 1). The condition before it keeps already-resting grains from moving again. This rule is intentionally constant-speed downward motion, matching the current game-design baseline; it is not an acceleration simulation. A physically named word such as gravity does not require pretending this simple rule is Newtonian integration.

sections.title: Make one function own the update rule
sections.html:
Put the mutation in tick_cell(&mut Cell, floor_row). Rendering receives only &Cell; tick_cell receives mutable access because it changes row. main keeps ownership. This connects the borrowing lesson to a concrete simulation boundary rather than introducing a new architecture vocabulary.

The same floor_row should determine both collision and the drawn floor position. If the visual floor uses an unrelated hardcoded y value, the grain may appear to hover or sink despite correct row arithmetic. One source of truth makes the relation between simulation and image inspectable.

sections.title: Test boundaries before looking at motion
sections.html:
Try rows 5,158 and159 with floor160. One tick should produce 8,159 and159 respectively. Those cases cover ordinary motion, a shortened final move and already-resting state. An invalid start such as row161 needs a separate rejection or recovery policy; do not silently call it a successful collision test.

The complete example below runs these cases through assertions. Then integrate it into the timed graphical program: draw the floor at floor_row times4, draw the grain from its current row, and use R to reset row5 and the teaching accumulator. A row5 to row159 fall needs 52 ticks because 51 full three-row moves reach158 and the final tick clamps to159.

sections.title: Know what this collision rule does not cover
sections.html:
Clamping against one horizontal floor works because we know the nearest relevant obstacle analytically. It does not prove safe movement through a general material world. If a stone occupies row157 and a grain starts at155, a three-row move must inspect the traversed path rather than only the floor or endpoint. The grid lesson will introduce those occupancy checks.

For the episode, show the failure by first allowing an unclamped step and placing the grain two rows above the floor. Then derive the fix from the last legal row. The visual is useful because it exposes the exact off-by-one boundary; the code should follow the picture, not appear as an unexplained min call.

16.outcome: Represent every valid prototype material with an enum and handle each case explicitly.
16.why: The world is about to contain air, sand and stone rather than one special grain. Raw numbers could label them, but numbers permit meaningless states and hide intent. An enum gives the domain a vocabulary the compiler can check.

sections.title: Replace implicit numeric meaning with named alternatives
sections.html:
Define Material with Air,Sand,Stone. Each variant is a valid alternative of the same type. A grid slot can hold one of these values; it cannot accidentally hold material17 unless we deliberately add such a representation. The benefit is not decorative naming: functions can demand Material rather than accepting every integer as potentially meaningful.

A custom enum can derive Copy,Clone,Debug,PartialEq,Eq when its contents support them. Here the variants carry no owned heap data, so those derived capabilities are appropriate. Deriving Copy is a deliberate modeling choice for a small material identity, unlike cloning an entire world to escape ownership design.

sections.title: Use match as a complete decision table
sections.html:
A match expression inspects the variant and selects its arm. Our example maps each material to a printable label. Later the same structure can select colour or movement kind. Because we list the variants explicitly, adding Water makes the compiler reveal match expressions that need another case.

Avoid adding a wildcard arm merely to silence that feedback when every known material needs intentional handling. A wildcard is useful when all remaining alternatives genuinely share one behavior, but it can also conceal an incomplete rule. Decide based on the domain contract, not on the shortest way to make a diagnostic disappear.

sections.title: Keep identity separate from state
sections.html:
Material::Sand identifies the kind of matter; a cell’s moisture and temperature describe its current state. We will not create a separate enum variant for every possible temperature. That would combine independent axes into an unmanageable list. A later cell struct stores identity and state separately.

For today, keep the enum small enough to enumerate in a terminal fixture. Draw each variant with one flat colour after the match behavior is understood. Air means an empty simulation slot, not an invisible solid; its visual background comes from the sky/interior rendering layer.

sections.title: Grow the table by observing a missing case
sections.html:
Add Water temporarily and run cargo check before implementing its label or colour. The non-exhaustive-match error is evidence that the compiler noticed a new domain alternative. Add an intentional arm and rerun. Then use equality to compare two Material values and Debug formatting to inspect them.

This gives us three useful tools: a closed set of names, exhaustive behavior selection, and simple diagnostics. The material table will grow, but the underlying reason stays the same: invalid combinations should be harder to represent, and missing behavior should be visible during development.

17.outcome: Store a small world in a persistent vector and initialize it with air plus a stone floor.
17.why: A pile needs many occupied and empty slots. A Vec owns a runtime-sized sequence of same-type elements, which gives us a compact first grid. We will separate allocation, initialization and drawing so the world is not silently recreated every frame.

sections.title: Allocate slots, not separate loose variables
sections.html:
A 32 by18 teaching world has576 slots. vec![Material::Air; width * height] creates that many initialized elements. Because Material is Copy, the repeated initialization is straightforward. The vector’s length counts valid elements; its capacity describes reserved storage and is not a list of additional cells you may index.

Use usize for dimensions and indices local to this nonnegative buffer. World coordinates will stay signed until validated. That distinction avoids converting negative positions into enormous unsigned indices. The next lesson implements the conversion boundary rather than scattering unchecked casts around the renderer.

sections.title: Store dimensions with the collection
sections.html:
Define World with width,height,cells. Keeping dimensions beside storage makes row-major mapping meaningful. A vector alone does not know whether576 items represent32×18,24×24 or one long column. The World interface supplies that interpretation.

A still scene might look identical even if reallocated repeatedly, but motion would reset and allocation cost would grow. 18.outcome: Convert signed cell coordinates into an Option index, rejecting invalid positions before casting.
18.why: Brushes and camera motion can produce coordinates outside the stored rectangle. A direct index formula is valid only inside its domain. We will derive both the row-major mapping and the validation order, so an edge click becomes an ordinary missing cell instead of a panic or unintended edit.

sections.title: Flatten one row at a time
sections.html:
In an eight-wide grid, row0 occupies indices0–7, row1 occupies8–15, and row2 occupies16–23. Each complete row skips width slots. Therefore the index is row*width+column. The width, not height, is the stride because adjacent columns are stored consecutively.

This derivation lets you reconstruct the formula instead of memorizing it. For a32×18 grid, the final valid coordinate31,17 maps to17*32+31=575, and the vector has576 elements. The final index is one less than the count because indexing begins at zero.

sections.title: Validate the signed inputs first
sections.html:
A valid column is at least0 and less than width; a valid row is at least0 and less than height. Test all four conditions while coordinates are still signed. A negative coordinate is not a valid usize, and casting it first does not preserve its intended meaning.

The helper returns None for positions outside the rectangle. For valid positions it returns Some(index). This signature makes absence explicit. It does not promise that every caller coordinate can be used. A later lesson will match these two alternatives instead of unwrapping blindly.

sections.title: Keep arithmetic assumptions in the contract
sections.html:
The focused helper uses positive i32 dimensions and small fixtures. Production world constructors should validate dimensions and checked multiplication before allocation so width*height cannot overflow. The example converts each nonnegative component to usize before computing the flat index.

Do not silently claim a helper is universally safe merely because it contains one bounds check. Its safety depends on the dimensions, allocation and coordinate representation agreeing. Store dimensions in one validated World and ensure cells.len()==width*height at construction; otherwise a geometrically valid coordinate could still address a mismatched buffer.

sections.title: Test corners and the first invalid positions
sections.html:
Check0,0;31,0;0,17;31,17, then -1,0;32,0;0,-1;0,18. These cases reveal sign errors, off-by-one boundaries and a mistaken stride. A center-cell test alone would miss most of those failures.

Use the same helper for drawing queries, movement and painting where the storage rectangle applies. That centralizes the domain decision. For an infinite chunked world, the mapping will first select a chunk and then validate or derive local coordinates; this bounded helper remains useful within each buffer.

19.outcome: Handle Some and None explicitly so an invalid brush coordinate becomes a safe no-op.
19.why: Our index helper now tells the truth: some positions do not name a stored cell. That result is only useful if the caller respects it. Matching Option turns a potential panic into an explicit choice at the boundary between user input and world mutation.

sections.title: A possible index is not an index yet
sections.html:
Option has two alternatives: Some carries a valid usize, while None carries no index. You cannot use the Option itself to index a vector because it is not a guarantee of a position. The caller must inspect the alternative and decide what absence means for its operation.

For painting just outside the view, doing nothing is reasonable. For a fixture that claims a known-valid position, absence may indicate a broken test setup and should fail loudly. The same type can support different policies; what matters is that the policy is visible rather than hidden in an arbitrary fallback number.

sections.title: Match binds the carried value
sections.html:
In match index(...) { Some(i) => ..., None => ... }, the Some arm introduces i for the carried index. That binding exists only in the arm where the value is present. The None arm cannot refer to a nonexistent index.

Use the successful arm to mutate one slot and the missing arm to return false. The bool result lets the caller report whether a paint command affected the stored rectangle. This is already a useful interface for tests and later input feedback. It avoids giving every caller direct access to unchecked vector indexing.

sections.title: Why index zero is not a fallback
sections.html:
Index0 is the top-left valid slot. Converting None into0 would turn an out-of-bounds brush stroke into a real edit at the world origin. That failure might appear as mysterious sand or erasure in the corner, far from the cursor. A numeric sentinel is safe only if the domain excludes it and every caller obeys the convention; our vector domain does not exclude0.

Likewise, unwrap on an ordinary edge click turns an expected condition into a panic. unwrap can be reasonable in a tightly controlled test whose setup guarantees Some, but it is not a substitute for defining runtime input behavior.

sections.title: Exercise both branches, not only the happy path
sections.html:
Use a tiny vector with a distinctive first value. Paint a valid coordinate, then try a negative coordinate and a coordinate exactly at width. Assert the invalid attempts return false and the first value is unchanged. This directly protects against the index-zero fallback bug.

Later, Option will recur in map lookups, neighbour searches and collision queries. The transferable idea is to distinguish “there is a value” from “there may be a value,” then choose the missing-case behavior according to the operation’s contract.

20.outcome: Transfer a grain into empty space without creating or destroying a copy.
20.why: Changing a destination cell to Sand looks like movement only if the source stops being sand. A swap expresses the full occupancy transfer and avoids holding two simultaneous mutable element references while the vector is owned by one world.

sections.title: State the conservation promise first
sections.html:
In a closed fixture with no painting, reactions or outflow, the number of sand cells should stay constant. That is the behavior we want before choosing an implementation. If a source contains Sand and a destination contains Air, the next state should contain Air at the source and Sand at the destination.

Writing only destination=Sand duplicates matter because the old source remains occupied. Clearing only the source destroys it. A visual test might still show a grain in roughly the right place, so count conservation is a separate assertion rather than something inferred from appearance.

sections.title: Use values for inspection, then one mutation
sections.html:
Because Material identity is Copy, read the two identities into local values or compare them through indexing. Once the movement condition is established, call cells.swap(source,destination). This exchanges the elements under one mutable access to the vector.

Trying to create &mut cells[source] and &mut cells[destination] simultaneously can be rejected because generic indices may coincide and the compiler cannot assume they are disjoint. swap is a standard interface whose implementation handles the aliasing contract. Use a safe operation that matches the intended transfer instead of reaching for unsafe pointers.

sections.title: Validate both indices before moving
sections.html:
The focused example uses two known-valid indices in a tiny vector. Runtime coordinates still pass through the checked mapping or world query. Moving from a source to itself should be either rejected or a documented no-op; it is not a successful fall. A blocked destination must leave both slots unchanged.

The movement helper returns bool to report whether it actually moved. That result will later help mark dirty rectangles or count activity. Do not infer success merely because the function was called. A movement attempt can fail for a normal reason such as a stone or occupied slot.

sections.title: Test state before and after the complete operation
sections.html:
Count Sand before the attempt, inspect the source/destination after it, and compare the count. Then run blocked, wrong-source and same-index cases. These tests describe the operation’s contract independently of its implementation.

When density exchanges arrive, a swap remains useful: heavier matter moves down while lighter matter takes its previous place. The condition becomes richer, but the paired occupancy transfer still must be complete. The simple Air/Sand fixture is therefore a foundation, not a disposable trick.

21.outcome: Inspect and count world contents through borrowed iteration while preserving the world for later frames.
21.why: A renderer and a statistics pass need to read all cells repeatedly. Rust offers several ways to iterate, and choosing the wrong ownership mode can consume the collection. We will compare those modes by their access contract, not by memorizing three similar names.

sections.title: Read elements without consuming storage
sections.html:
cells.iter() produces shared references to the vector’s elements. The vector remains owned by World. This is the natural starting point for counting materials or drawing cells, because neither task should take the collection away from the simulation.

A for loop over &cells also borrows its contents. The exact binding type inside the loop matters: with an iterator over references, a value comparison may need dereferencing. Begin with explicit for syntax and print the types mentally before compressing it into chained operations. Concision is useful only after the ownership relation is clear.

sections.title: Mutable iteration grants field access, not resizing permission
sections.html:
iter_mut() lends mutable access to elements one by one. It suits an operation such as setting a local flag or resetting a numeric buffer. While such borrows are in use, you cannot freely resize the same vector because reallocation could invalidate references.

Use a fixed-size cell buffer for a simulation pass and separate additions/removals into another owned event list when needed. A grid neighbour-movement pass may be clearer with indices and controlled swaps rather than iter_mut, because it needs to access related slots and avoid aliasing. There is no rule that every loop must be rewritten as an iterator chain.

sections.title: Consuming iteration is a different operation
sections.html:
Calling into_iter on an owned Vec consumes the collection and yields owned elements. That can be exactly right when transferring or transforming ownership, but it is wrong for a renderer that must use the same world again next frame. Calling methods on a borrowed value can have different receiver behavior, so inspect the actual receiver type rather than memorizing the method name alone.

The focused example uses a borrowed iter twice to prove the vector survives both passes. Then a separate temporary vector can demonstrate consuming iteration. Do not consume the main world just to print it and then recreate it, because that hides the architectural mistake with unnecessary allocation.

sections.title: Derive counts as observations, not additional state
sections.html:
A sand count can be computed from the existing cells by filtering identities. It need not be maintained as a second mutable truth until performance measurements justify a cached counter. Two independent counts that can drift make conservation harder to reason about.

Use enumeration when you need each element’s flat index, then derive row and column from that index and width. That makes drawing a read-only interpretation of storage. End with a prediction: adding one Sand through an explicit paint command changes the observed count by one; drawing and counting alone leave it unchanged.

22.outcome: Guarantee a grain receives at most one movement update per simulation tick.
22.why: An in-place scan changes the collection it is still traversing. A moved grain may land in a slot the scan has not visited yet and move again immediately. The bug is about update order, so we will make that order visible in a tiny column before adding chunks.

sections.title: Construct the counterexample
sections.html:
Place one grain at the top of a six-cell column and scan from top to bottom. At row0 it moves to1; the scan next reaches row1 and sees the same grain again. It may fall through the entire column in one tick even though the rule promised one step. Counting grains does not catch this because mass is conserved while timing is wrong.

Trace the occupied row after every scan position. The problem is not gravity strength or elapsed-time scheduling; it is that a single material instance is being selected repeatedly during one update. This distinction prevents tuning a speed constant to conceal an update-order bug.

sections.title: Reverse the falling scan
sections.html:
For downward movement, scan bottom to top. A grain moves into a slot that was already visited during this pass, so the simple one-row example cannot be encountered again. In a flat row-major buffer, visit higher row indices first.

This is helpful but not the final guarantee. Multiple phases, horizontal movement and chunk boundaries can still allow a later traversal to see the moved cell. The game therefore also needs a moved-this-tick marker with a precisely defined reset policy. The marker belongs to material state and must travel with the grain during a swap.

sections.title: Define marker ownership and reset
sections.html:
For the focused experiment use a Cell with occupied and moved fields. Clear moved at the start of the tick, then mark the destination after a transfer. Any later attempt skips a moved cell. In production, an update parity bit can avoid clearing every field, but parity must be handled carefully when frozen cells return and must not accidentally mark newborn or reactivated cells forever.

The code below demonstrates a single pass explicitly. Do not optimize marker storage before proving the once-per-tick property. A tiny test can record the grain’s displacement and catch repeated moves even when the final image still looks plausible.

sections.title: Extend the assertion across boundaries
sections.html:
When chunks are introduced, place the source on the last row or column of a chunk and run the same movement limit assertion across the neighbour boundary. Retain the marker across all phases in a tick, not reset independently when each chunk starts.

The acceptance promise is about one logical update, not one function call or one storage object. A bottom-to-top scan is a strategy; a traveled-distance/marker test checks the actual promise. Keep both location and conservation assertions because they protect different bugs.

23.outcome: Create sand piles and a bounded water-leveling rule while preventing directional bias.
23.why: Falling straight down cannot build a sloped pile or spread a pool. We need alternative destinations when the cell below is blocked. Powder and liquid movement share occupancy queries but have different fallback rules, so material kind must guide the candidate search.

sections.title: Start from the blocked downward case
sections.html:
First attempt the approved downward path. If it is blocked, sand may try downward diagonals subject to its repose rule; water may also search sideways through free or eligible slots. Candidate destinations are not permission to teleport through intervening walls. Every larger move must inspect its path.

Build a tiny stone bowl with one narrow column of sand or water above it. This fixture is more informative than an infinite flat floor because it creates blocked, diagonal, sideways and contained cases close together. Use the same fixture for before/after counts so leaks are visible.

sections.title: Distinguish powder slopes from liquid leveling
sections.html:
A powder pile needs a stability criterion, not endless diagonal drifting. The game design names a repose-angle rule, which should be approved and tested at cell scale. Water aims to flatten within its connected basin, but the initial bounded sideways search is an approximation rather than a pressure solver.

Do not claim a two-candidate toy rule already implements realistic fluid mechanics. It is a small readable rule that produces the game’s desired visible behavior. Write down the maximum search distance and the blocked-path condition. Those bounds become part of the later thread footprint proof and performance budget.

sections.title: Remove a permanent left-first preference
sections.html:
If every cell tries left before right, symmetric scenes can develop a persistent left bias. Alternate preference deterministically using step count or an approved coordinate hash. Deterministic alternation gives varied choices without depending on thread timing or a global RNG consumed in an unstable order.

The focused helper below chooses between two known-eligible candidates. It is not the entire liquid rule. Its job is to expose the tie-break policy: when both exist, choose according to the current parity; when only one exists, choose it; when neither exists, report no move.

sections.title: Judge the complete pile and pool contracts

The rendering frame should show the latest state independently of movement frequency. If the pool behaves differently merely because the camera redraws faster, return to the tick scheduler rather than retuning sideways reach. Storage, scheduling and material policy should remain separate causes you can inspect.
