24.outcome: Convert cursor positions into cell edits and prevent painting outside the world view.
24.why: The sandbox begins when the player can place matter. Mouse input lives in drawing coordinates, while world storage uses cell coordinates. A careful conversion and input ownership rule keep a click from painting the wrong slot or leaking through UI panels.

sections.title: Read input as a request, not direct world mutation
sections.html:
macroquad provides mouse_position and button state queries. A held button means the player may want repeated paint actions; a just-pressed query means an event begins once. Choose the query according to the tool: continuous painting differs from a one-shot command.

First log the drawing coordinates or show a simple cursor marker. Do not immediately cast them into vector indices. A position outside the world, including negative values or UI borders, is a normal input case and must be rejected or consumed before reaching storage.

sections.title: Invert the drawing transform
sections.html:
If drawing a cell uses screen_x=view_origin_x+(world_x-camera_x)*cell_size, picking reverses that relationship. Subtract the view origin, divide by cell size, take the appropriate floor, then add the camera coordinate. In the initial no-camera window, that reduces to floor(mouse_x/4).

Check that the cursor is inside the view rectangle before converting. Truncating a small negative float toward zero can otherwise paint column0 even though the cursor lies outside the world. The focused helper validates first, then floors. Production physical-pixel/DPI conversion is another boundary, not a reason to mix raw framebuffer and logical mouse units.

sections.title: Use one paint command for input and tests
sections.html:
Define a paint operation receiving validated coordinates, selected material and brush settings. Both the mouse handler and headless fixtures should call that operation. This prevents tests from bypassing the actual edit policy. Normal paint replaces the covered cells; the later Alt mode fills air only.

For the first one-cell brush, left hold paints sand and right hold paints air. Decide priority if both buttons are held. Ignore events consumed by UI before sending a world command. Even before the final HUD exists, keep this ordering explicit so the first swatch click does not also modify the world underneath.

sections.title: Check continuity and boundaries
sections.html:
A mouse can move several cells between frames. Painting only the current point leaves gaps during fast drags; the later brush stroke should rasterize the segment between successive sampled points. Start by documenting that limitation, then add a bounded line traversal rather than increasing frame rate to hide it.

Test every view edge, a negative position, a coordinate exactly at width and a click over a mock UI rectangle. The result should be a predictable brush footprint with no edits outside the intended region. Cursor display is feedback; it should use the same conversion as the actual paint operation.

25.outcome: Separate world storage, simulation and rendering into modules with narrow interfaces.
25.why: Our main file now contains unrelated reasons to change: storage layout, falling rules, mouse handling and drawing. Modules let us separate those responsibilities so a physics test can run without opening a window and a visual change cannot casually rewrite state.

sections.title: Begin with dependencies, not folder decoration
sections.html:
World stores material state. Simulation reads and updates it. Rendering reads it. Main coordinates input, scheduling and presentation. Draw these relationships before moving files: the useful boundary is which operations need ownership or mutation, not how many folders look professional.

A module is a namespace and visibility boundary. Splitting code into files without changing who can touch what can merely scatter the same coupling. Start with world.rs, simulation.rs and render.rs only because those jobs already exist in the program.

sections.title: Expose operations rather than every field
sections.html:
Rust items are private by default in the relevant module context. Use pub on the small interfaces another module genuinely needs. A render function may accept &World, a tick function &mut World. The rest of the crate should not require direct mutable access to every allocation detail.

Early teaching code may temporarily expose fields while we learn the mechanics, but record that as a convenience rather than a final design principle. A checked query and paint/move operation can preserve invariants better than callers independently calculating unchecked indices.

sections.title: Move one responsibility and compile
sections.html:
Create world.rs with the material/world definitions, declare mod world; in the crate root, and import the needed public type. Compile before moving the next responsibility. This isolates missing visibility and path errors. A huge simultaneous file shuffle makes it harder to distinguish an architecture mistake from a simple import typo.

The worked terminal example below demonstrates a nested module in one file so it can be compiled independently. The same module body can move to src/world.rs when the crate root declares mod world. File location follows Rust’s module rules; a file merely existing in src does not automatically make its items available.

sections.title: Protect the headless path
sections.html:
Keep window initialization in main and graphical drawing in render. A test of World or tick should not invoke macroquad’s main attribute or create a native context. This reduces setup cost and lets CI exercise behavior without a display.

Do not introduce traits or generics at every boundary just because modules exist. A small concrete function can be a strong interface. We will add a trait later where interchangeable deterministic choice sources create a real testing need. End the episode with one headless test importing the simulation path and one working window using the same state model.

26.outcome: Write headless tests that detect a movement regression and distinguish compilation from behavioral proof.
26.why: cargo check tells us that code satisfies Rust’s static rules, not that sand stops at the right place. A tiny deterministic fixture can express the game behavior we want and catch a later regression automatically without opening a window.

sections.title: Specify a visible promise as an assertion
sections.html:
Choose one concrete rule: a grain above the floor falls, a grain at the floor stays, and no step crosses the floor. Construct the smallest state that could violate it. Run the helper, then assert the resulting row. The test’s value comes from the counterexample it can reject, not from the number of assertions.

Avoid a test that simply reproduces the implementation arithmetic line-for-line and compares the same formula to itself. Use expected outcomes chosen from the behavior contract. For movement in a grid, also count conserved materials because a correct destination can coexist with a duplicated source.

sections.title: Use Rust’s test harness
sections.html:
A function marked #[test] is run by cargo test. Assertions panic when their condition fails, which the test harness reports as a failure. Put a tests module behind #[cfg(test)] so the tests belong to the relevant code without becoming the program’s entry behavior.

The worked example is a small library-style source file. Put it in src/lib.rs or the appropriate simulation module, then run cargo test. There is no graphical main or context. A passing test produces a concise test summary; it does not need to print a celebratory message from the game.

sections.title: Prove the test can catch the bug
sections.html:
Temporarily remove the destination clamp or change the floor offset, then run the relevant test by name. The expected failure demonstrates that the test is connected to the promise. Restore the implementation and rerun. A test suite that never fails under a known broken rule may be asserting the wrong observation.

Keep the deliberate failure out of the final working state. For a YouTube episode, the red-to-green moment makes the reason for testing concrete: the test protects an actual visible bug rather than satisfying a code-style ritual.

sections.title: Separate headless, visual and performance evidence
sections.html:
A headless assertion can verify exact positions, counts and deadlines in ticks. It cannot establish whether the effect is readable in a tiny muted-palette frame or whether it runs smoothly on the floor GPU. Those need their own manual and measured checks.

Use fixtures repeatedly across the course: controlled inputs, specified tick count, expected result. Later multi-seed reliability checks and cross-thread hashes will extend this foundation. Do not broaden tests simply to mirror every helper; keep meaningful behavioral invariants tied to the game’s acceptance conditions.

27.outcome: Use a coordinate-keyed map for sparse chunk storage while keeping update order explicit.
27.why: An explored world may contain far-apart regions. A giant vector spanning every coordinate between them would allocate empty space unnecessarily. A map stores only resident chunk keys, but its container iteration order must not accidentally become the simulation’s update order.

sections.title: Choose a key that names the storage unit
sections.html:
A chunk key can begin as a pair of signed integer coordinates, such as (chunk_x,chunk_y). The map associates that key with an owned Chunk value. Querying a missing key returns Option because absence is expected in a sparse procedural world. It does not automatically mean corruption or an error.

Start with a tiny payload such as a vector length or identifier before storing full chunks. This isolates insertion, lookup and removal from the movement rules. Then connect the same interface to real Chunk storage. Storage choices should not rewrite gravity or material identities.

sections.title: Understand ownership of entries
sections.html:
Inserting an owned Chunk transfers that value into the map. get lends shared access; get_mut lends mutable access to one existing value. Removing an entry returns ownership so it can be saved, discarded or transferred to a background job under the chosen policy.

A borrowed entry cannot remain live while you arbitrarily restructure the same map. Plan the operation in phases: identify keys, borrow the needed data, finish that access, then perform structural changes. Copying a small coordinate key is cheap and often clarifies this boundary; cloning every chunk to avoid borrows is not the same thing.

sections.title: Separate lookup structure from deterministic traversal
sections.html:
HashMap does not promise the stable iteration order required by our simulation contract. Collect active keys and sort them according to the explicit phase/scan plan before updating. Alternatively an ordered map may help for some traversal needs, but it still does not substitute for the specified four-phase ordering.

The focused example inserts keys in one order and prints them after sorting. A repeatable output demonstrates that update order can be defined independently of insertion order. Later the phase selector groups by coordinate parity, while per-chunk scan order follows the movement contract.

sections.title: Check sparse behavior and eviction readiness
sections.html:
Insert chunks at0,0 and100000,0. The map should contain two entries, not allocate the entire distance between them. Remove one and inspect the returned value. Before persistent saving exists, only unchanged regenerable chunks may be discarded; edited chunks must remain resident under the temporary M0 policy.

This lesson is about data organization, not a promise of infinite memory. The cache lesson will enforce a resident budget and the saving milestone will make edited eviction recoverable. A sparse map makes those policies possible but does not implement them by itself.

28.outcome: Map global cell positions into64×64 chunks correctly, including positions left of the origin.
28.why: Chunks let us bound allocation and reuse a fixed-size cell buffer. The subtle part is not allocating4096 slots; it is agreeing which chunk contains a negative coordinate. Euclidean quotient and remainder give a consistent answer that ordinary truncating division does not.

sections.title: Derive chunk and local coordinates
sections.html:
For nonnegative x, chunk_x counts how many complete groups of64 precede the cell, while local_x is its offset inside that group. x63 belongs to chunk0 at local63; x64 belongs to chunk1 at local0. The same idea must continue to the left of zero.

The cell immediately left of x0 is x-1. It belongs to chunk-1 at local63, not chunk0 at local-1. That keeps every local coordinate inside0..64 and every chunk a complete fixed-size rectangle. Draw the boundary on a number line before choosing an operator.

sections.title: Use Euclidean operations for signed world positions
sections.html:
Rust integer / truncates toward zero, which gives an inconvenient quotient for negative chunk mapping. Use div_euclid(64) and rem_euclid(64) with a positive chunk size. The quotient identifies the containing chunk and the remainder is nonnegative.

The round-trip equation is world_x=chunk_x*64+local_x. Test it for -65,-64,-1,0,63,64. This equation is a stronger check than a few printed labels because it proves the decomposition reconstructs each tested input. Use suitable world integer widths and checked range assumptions in production.

sections.title: Allocate one owned buffer per chunk
sections.html:
A Chunk owns4096 cells, indexed locally by local_y*64+local_x under a declared row convention. World storage maps a chunk key to that buffer. The global query first decomposes coordinates, finds or requests the chunk, and then addresses the local slot.

Keep missing chunk handling explicit. A query cannot silently fabricate changed data or treat missing storage as a solid wall in some paths and air in others. The generation/loading policy determines when a missing chunk becomes resident; movement and rendering should use that policy consistently.

sections.title: Preserve movement across the storage seam
sections.html:
Place a grain at the last local row of one chunk with free space in its neighbour. One logical move must transfer state across the boundary and retain its moved marker. Per-chunk reset or an unchecked local index can duplicate matter, panic or accelerate the grain.

Chunking is storage organization, not a new physical law. The grain should follow the same rule whether a boundary lies under it or not. Keep the first chunk traversal sequential and explicit; parallelism comes only after the cross-chunk footprint proof. Measure the extra lookup cost later instead of guessing that chunks are automatically faster.

29.outcome: Pan the visible world while simulating only the cell-clipped view plus its16-cell margin.
29.why: A camera changes which part of the world is visible, not the stored size of a grain. The active simulation region is the visible rectangle plus a small margin. Selecting overlapping chunks alone is too broad, so we will compute exact per-cell intersections.

sections.title: Write the camera transform in units
sections.html:
A camera origin identifies the world coordinate displayed at the view’s origin. Drawing subtracts that origin before multiplying by cell size. Picking reverses the transform. Use one shared conversion contract so moving the camera cannot separate cursor targeting from the image.

In this prototype, rows still increase downward; the later altitude lesson converts to the final upward-world convention. Keep that limitation visible. Camera easing may use fractional presentation state, but grid edits must resolve to explicit cell coordinates and drawing must preserve hard pixel edges.

sections.title: Define half-open rectangles
sections.html:
Represent a rectangle as left,top,right,bottom with right and bottom excluded. Its width is right-left and height bottom-top. Expanding the view by16 cells subtracts16 from left/top and adds16 to right/bottom. Intersection takes the greater lower bounds and smaller upper bounds.

Half-open ranges match Rust iteration and avoid double-updating a boundary cell shared by adjacent rectangles. Empty intersections are ordinary: if left>=right or top>=bottom, there are no cells to visit. The focused example computes these bounds independently of world storage so edge cases remain easy to test.

sections.title: Clip inside every overlapping chunk
sections.html:
A64-cell chunk that overlaps the active rectangle may extend63 extra cells beyond it. Updating that entire chunk reintroduces a much larger margin than the design budgets. The distinction between storage unit and simulation unit is crucial. A resident chunk can be partly active and partly frozen. Its allocation exists as a whole, but only the selected cells receive movement, heat and slow work under the current active-region policy.

30.outcome: Evict unchanged resident chunks under a memory budget without losing edited world state.
30.why: Chunking prevents one giant allocation, but keeping every visited chunk forever still grows memory. A resident cache needs a discard policy that respects which data can be regenerated and which data contains the player’s work.

sections.title: Classify what can be recovered
sections.html:
An unchanged chunk can be reconstructed from seed, coordinates and generator version. An edited or simulated changed chunk differs from that baseline. Before saving exists, discarding the latter loses information. Therefore M0 may drop only unchanged resident chunks; changed chunks stay resident under an explicitly documented temporary limitation.

This is a tradeoff, not the final bounded-memory design. M4 adds persistence so changed chunks can be evicted after a safe write. A cache policy must never silently redefine changed as “not currently visible” just to meet a memory cap.

sections.title: Track recency separately from activity
sections.html:
Active chunks are currently needed by the simulation rectangle and should not be eviction candidates. Resident inactive chunks are frozen and can be considered. A last-active sequence counter gives a deterministic recency ordering; least-recently-active unchanged chunks are the first candidates under the temporary policy.

Do not use wall-clock timestamps if a simple monotonic sequence expresses the needed order. Tie-break by chunk key so fixture results are stable. The focused example chooses one victim from metadata rather than mutating actual chunks, which isolates the policy from disk I/O and borrowing complexity.

sections.title: Budget bytes rather than guessing from count
sections.html:
A chunk’s cell payload has a measurable size, but the process also owns map entries, metadata, vectors, rendering resources and pending work. A nominal64MB chunk-data cap is not a promise that the whole application uses64MB. Record what the cap includes and measure total resident memory separately.

When no safe unchanged victim remains, report the temporary limitation during development instead of deleting edited state. That scenario belongs in a test because it is inevitable under sustained editing before persistence is implemented. A memory watchdog cannot substitute for a data-loss policy.

sections.title: Verify regeneration and preserve changed chunks
sections.html:
Pan through unchanged terrain and count resident chunks under a chosen small fixture budget. Revisit an evicted coordinate and verify deterministic regeneration. Then mark a chunk changed, make it least recent, and confirm it is not chosen by the M0 victim selector.

The final cache will coordinate with the single-writer save queue, but do not invent that mechanism before the persistence lessons. A good incremental course names temporary restrictions clearly so the learner understands what is finished, what is safe, and which later module removes the limitation.

31.outcome: Record repeatable tick, frame and memory measurements and make an evidence-based M0 decision.
31.why: A simulation that looks smooth on a modern laptop may fail on the target i3. We need a repeatable workload and separate measurements for a tick and the whole rendered frame. This module closes the foundation only when its claims have actual evidence.

sections.title: Freeze the workload before measuring
sections.html:
Use fixed dimensions, seed, camera, material counts and input sequence. The i3 reference active load is74624 cells at the specified720p view with margins; the reference1080p load is154624. Include a sand fixture and a50%-water fixture. State exactly which cells are active rather than quoting only visible counts.

Before this benchmark, the sequential four-phase chunk traversal should exist so the measured algorithm matches the intended update order. Keep it single-threaded until a footprint proof and measurement justify parallel dispatch. Benchmarking a different toy traversal would not establish the proposed architecture’s cost.

sections.title: Measure tick time and frame time separately
sections.html:
Use Instant around simulation work and around the complete frame’s CPU work, with a documented sampling interval. A20TPS simulation can still hitch if one synchronous tick takes40ms. Multiple ticks in one frame must be budgeted together. Record distributions or at least average and worst observed values, not only a flattering mean.

GPU presentation and OS scheduling can complicate frame measurement, so state what the timer includes. Do not label a CPU-only duration as complete display latency. The initial goal is honest comparable evidence, not a profiler dashboard with unexplained numbers.

sections.title: Use optimized builds and real hardware
sections.html:
Run cargo run --release for performance measurements. Debug builds are useful for development but not the agreed optimized performance target. Record CPU model, memory, OS, graphics device, resolution and build revision with the results. If the exact floor machine is unavailable, mark the result unverified rather than extrapolating a certification from the Mac.

Check that the graphics context opens and draws on that target GPU before spending weeks on more reactions. A supported-platform list does not prove old integrated graphics compatibility. If the floor fails, revise the target or renderer through an explicit design decision.

sections.title: Turn the measurement into a gate
sections.html:
The M0 report should answer: does sand meet the target, what do water timings show, is memory bounded under the current policy, and are threads needed next? Keep failing evidence and the selected response in the report. Dirty regions, a smaller capped view or later threading are options to evaluate, not invisible changes to acceptance conditions.

The worked timing fixture below demonstrates measurement mechanics only; its tiny synthetic loop is not a substitute for the real sand/water benchmark. End the episode with a reproducible command and a table of actual results, including any unresolved hardware access. Completion means making the decision honestly, not forcing every number green.

32.outcome: Separate shared material properties from per-cell state and measure the actual proposed cell layout.
32.why: Two sand cells have the same material conductivity but can have different temperatures and moisture. Mixing those concepts wastes storage and obscures rules. We will put stable properties in a lookup and changing state in each cell, then check the real size rather than trusting a field-size sum.

sections.title: Ask what varies between cells of one material
sections.html:
Density, nominal conductivity, porosity and ignition threshold describe a material kind. Temperature, moisture, progress, timers and flags describe one cell now. A property lookup takes Material and returns its shared configuration; the cell stores only the material identity needed to select it.

This is a data-modeling decision with a direct memory consequence. Copying an entire property table into each cell increases memory without adding information. Conversely, storing one global temperature per material would prevent hot and cold instances from coexisting. Keep identity, shared rules and current state separate.

sections.title: Use signed temperature and bounded moisture
sections.html:
The design uses signed i16 temperature so subzero states and lava temperatures fit its chosen range. Moisture has a documented0–100 meaning, while u8 can represent more values; the type alone does not enforce that smaller domain. Clamp or validate transitions through a narrow operation rather than scattering unchecked writes.

The timer/progress/flag fields also need explicit meaning per material. A phase conversion should clear stale state that no longer applies. Adding a field because there is a spare byte is not enough; define who updates it, under which clock and how it survives movement or save/load.

sections.title: Measure layout rather than summing field widths
sections.html:
The proposed fields add up to8 bytes, but Rust struct layout can include alignment and padding, and default representation is not a stable disk protocol. Use size_of and align_of to inspect the actual selected definition. If the result misses the budget, investigate field ordering or a deliberate representation choice with tests.

Do not serialize raw struct memory as the public save format merely because its measured size is8. Padding, representation guarantees, invalid enum values and future changes make explicit encoding a separate responsibility. Today’s measurement is about in-memory budget, not compatibility.

sections.title: Give the rule table a small tested interface
sections.html:
Start with Air,Sand,Water,Stone and properties needed by the next density/heat fixtures. Return a compact property value by matching Material. Test that two cells of the same identity can retain different temperatures while reading identical conductivity.

For Air, the current design reads ambient rather than storing meaningful per-cell temperature. Keep that exception explicit so empty space does not accidentally participate in the same stored-temperature rule. The worked example demonstrates separation and size inspection; the final packed layout remains subject to the actual implementation’s constraints.

33.outcome: Exchange sand, water and oil according to approved kind/density rules without passing through rigid solids.
33.why: The air-only prototype cannot show sand sinking in water or oil floating above it. Density exchange extends movement while preserving both materials. But a numeric density comparison alone is insufficient: it must also respect material kind and structural rules.

sections.title: Describe the intended exchange
sections.html:
If sand lies above water, the approved powder/fluid rule can move sand down and displace water upward. If oil lies above water, the lighter oil should not sink by the same downward exchange. A stable layered fixture makes those expectations explicit before code.

Use a consistent numeric scale for density values. The worked example uses small integer-relative values; the absolute unit is irrelevant to the ordering, but comparing quantities from inconsistent scales would be a bug. The material table and property lookup should define that convention once.

sections.title: Constrain which kinds may exchange
sections.html:
A dense stone cell should not automatically pass through another rigid solid or ignore its support group. Eligibility depends on kind and the relevant movement rule as well as density. Our focused function allows a moving powder/liquid to exchange only into air or eligible liquid under the chosen ordering.

That contract is a teaching baseline, not a complete buoyancy solver. Rigid-group flotation is handled later at group level. Keep separate systems separate: a property lookup can supply density, but it does not decide every motion consequence by itself.

sections.title: Preserve the paired state transfer
sections.html:
When an exchange is eligible, swap the complete cell state, not just material identity if temperature/moisture belong to the matter. Moving Sand identity while leaving its temperature behind would teleport heat between materials. Timers, progress and moved markers need equally explicit transfer semantics.

The worked fixture swaps enum values to isolate eligibility. Integrate it by moving the production Cell state consistently and marking the destination as updated. For a longer downward path, test each traversed location and apply a defined sequence; do not inspect only the final cell and leap through a wall.

sections.title: Test both motion and stability
sections.html:
Build closed columns for sand-over-water, oil-over-water and water-over-oil. Run the update enough times to see the selected ordering, then verify it remains stable under the same rule. Count each material before and after. A stable image without counts can hide duplication; preserved counts without expected ordering can hide a blocked exchange.

Also test Stone as an intervening blocker. That is the counterexample that prevents a naive “greater density always swaps” rule from taking over structural physics. The course’s goal is visibly consistent game behavior, not an unqualified claim of realistic fluid simulation.

34.outcome: Exchange heat across one closed edge with stable direction and paired accounting.
34.why: A lava reaction depends on heat moving between cells, but a full landscape makes a faulty transfer hard to diagnose. Start with two cells. If the pair has no external source or sink, one cell’s gain should correspond to the other’s loss under the selected model.

sections.title: Name the model before the formula
sections.html:
Our initial fixture gives the two cells equal heat capacity and uses integer temperature-like values. Under that simplified assumption, equal-and-opposite temperature changes preserve the pair’s sum. Real materials with different heat capacities require a more careful energy model; do not label this fixture a complete thermodynamic simulation.

The purpose is to establish update direction, bounded transfer and scan consistency. Hotter should cool, colder should warm, and equal values should remain equal. A transfer rate must not overshoot equilibrium and make the cells oscillate merely because the update was applied too aggressively.

sections.title: Read the old pair, then apply both changes
sections.html:
Compute the transfer from the two old values. Add it to the cooler cell and subtract it from the warmer. Do not update the first and then use that already-changed number as the second cell’s old state. That creates scan-order dependence and can break accounting.

For a multi-neighbour grid, choose an explicit old-state/delta scheme or another justified update method. The pair fixture does not automatically prove all neighbour interactions are safe. Write the full per-tick read/write footprint before combining this with parallel chunk scheduling.

sections.title: Make rounding a documented policy
sections.html:
Integer storage forces small transfers to round. A deterministic floor may eventually stall near equilibrium; randomized rounding may reduce that bias but needs the coordinate/step-based RNG contract. Choose the policy deliberately and test its consequences. The example below uses a bounded integer quarter-difference transfer as a readable fixture.

It preserves the pair’s sum and never reverses hot/cold ordering, but it can stop when the difference is below4. That limitation is visible and acceptable for the teaching experiment; production tuning must meet the required visible reaction deadlines and define behavior at the stored temperature resolution.

sections.title: Separate closed accounting from sources and ambient
sections.html:
A closed pair test excludes lava source maintenance, burning fuel, ambient exchange and phase-change policies. Those may intentionally add, remove or transform heat under the game’s approximations. Keep source/sink terms explicit so a conservation assertion is applied only where its assumptions hold.

Test the pair in both orientations, at equality and near the integer rounding threshold. Then integrate a small row fixture with a fixed update scheme. End the episode by showing that reversing storage order does not reverse the physical direction of transfer or create heat under the closed-fixture rules.

35.outcome: Implement separate sky-exposure and air-contact queries so shelter and cooling do not contradict each other.
35.why: A roof should block rain while the room beneath it can still contain air. A cave wall should exchange heat with nearby air without being directly exposed to the sky. One generic exposed flag cannot answer both questions, so we will separate their geometry and test the difference.

sections.title: Ask two different questions
sections.html:
Sky-exposed asks whether the cell is at the relevant top surface with an unobstructed direct-weather route under the game’s column model. Air-exposed asks whether at least one neighbouring location contains air. The first controls direct precipitation and sunlight; the second controls local heat exchange.

A cave wall can satisfy air contact while failing sky exposure. A roof’s top may be sky-exposed while its underside shelters the contents. These are not contradictory states; they describe different relationships. Naming them separately prevents a fix for rain from accidentally stopping all cave cooling.

sections.title: Define what the surface map includes
sections.html:
The current design’s surface heightmap counts settled blocking cells and ignores falling drops and plants for its base terrain surface semantics. Otherwise a raindrop would repeatedly become the highest non-gas cell and make terrain exposure flicker. Attached plant precipitation handling is a separate rule rather than an accidental heightmap side effect.

When a blocking cell is added above the current surface, update the column height. Removing the current surface requires finding the next valid blocker below. That search needs bounded storage/loading semantics in the vertically bounded world; do not assume a missing loaded chunk proves an unobstructed infinite column.

sections.title: Implement local contact independently
sections.html:
A four-neighbour air query checks the nearby cells that exchange heat under the chosen grid rule. It does not need to scan to the sky. At an active/storage boundary, use the explicit world-query policy rather than silently treating every absent allocation as ambient air.

The focused example uses a small hand-built roof and wall fixture, with a surface map derived from solid cells only. It prints the two predicates for a cell below the roof. Production will use the approved settled/material flags, but the central distinction remains the same: local contact and global column shelter are separate queries.

sections.title: Verify with counterexamples, not only open ground
sections.html:
Test an open surface, a roofed interior, a cave wall, a falling drop and a canopy. Confirm that drops do not rewrite the terrain surface and that shelter prevents direct precipitation without disabling all air contact. Include a roof edit so the cached surface map updates when geometry changes.

M1 can use fixed ambient inputs and handcrafted geometry; the live seasonal clock and procedural generator arrive later. That sequencing lets us prove the exposure contract before adding weather fields or large terrain. End the episode by tracing the same cell through a roof removal and explaining which predicate changes and why.

worked.label: Complete focused example — src/main.rs
worked.expected: wall: sheltered from sky, touching air. This focused fixture uses downward rows; production altitude conversion is taught later.
explanation: The fixture deliberately separates geometry predicates from weather/temperature values.
Missing neighbours are not automatically declared air here; production must define its boundary query policy.
Surface-map inclusion and attached-plant rain handling are separate contracts.

exercises.title: Remove the roof
exercises.prompt: Clear the upper solid, rebuild the surface column and recheck the wall.
exercises.hint: The next blocker becomes the column’s surface.
exercises.solution: The wall at row3 becomes the highest blocker in that column, so sky_exposed becomes true. Air contact can remain true. The two predicates need not change together.
exercises.proof: Cached geometry updates after the actual edit.

exercises.title: Add a falling drop conceptually
exercises.prompt: Should a moving raindrop above the roof redefine the settled terrain surface?
exercises.hint: The map’s inclusion rule is part of its contract.
exercises.solution: No under the current settled-surface design. Precipitation and moving matter need their own handling; including every transient cell would make shelter tests unstable.
exercises.proof: You explain the membership rule rather than relying on gas/non-gas alone.

exercises.title: Test a sealed interior cell
exercises.prompt: Surround a solid cell with non-air neighbours while keeping it below a roof.
exercises.hint: Local air contact requires at least one actual air neighbour.
exercises.solution: Both predicates can be false: it is sheltered and has no air-contact neighbour. Heat exchange with non-air neighbours remains a separate rule and should still run.
exercises.proof: The test does not equate lack of ambient contact with lack of all heat conduction.

troubleshooting.symptom: Rain flickers between ground and drops
troubleshooting.cause: Transient falling cells were included in the surface map.
troubleshooting.fix: Apply the settled/material inclusion contract explicitly.

troubleshooting.symptom: Lava in a cave never cools
troubleshooting.cause: Sky exposure was incorrectly used as the only air-contact test.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a separate local air-exposed predicate and sheltered ambient policy.

troubleshooting.symptom: Roof removal leaves the room permanently sheltered
troubleshooting.cause: The cached surface column was not updated.
troubleshooting.fix: Recompute the affected column under a bounded storage query and test edit invalidation.

episode.hook: A roof should block rain while the room beneath it can still contain air. A cave wall should exchange heat with nearby air without being directly exposed to the sky. One generic exposed flag cannot answer both questions, so we will separate their geometry and test the difference.
beats: Ask two different questions
Define what the surface map includes
Implement local contact independently
Verify with counterexamples, not only open ground
episode.demo: Implement separate sky-exposure and air-contact queries so shelter and cooling do not contradict each other.
episode.recap: Explain the result without reading the code, make one predicted change, then show the observed result.
